A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SoSBench benchmark and data-evolution framework. The complete main texts and appendices, including tables, figures and equations, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, scaling and unlearning experiments, human-referenced evaluator comparisons, and jailbreak results in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations and additional benchmark characterization, full-versus-Lite comparisons, and multi-turn jailbreak experiments in Section 4 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction algorithm, prompt mutation and coverage-driven sampling remain unchanged. The custom scoring component changes from GPT-4.1 with safe/unsafe output to GPT-5 with revised operational-enablement rules, refusal subtypes and a rationale (v1 Figure 8; v3 Figure 9). This revises the judge rather than the core data-synthesis algorithm.

E1.justification: The six scientific domains, 3,000-prompt benchmark, 300-prompt Lite subset and MMLU coverage remain. v3 adds adversarial multi-turn dialogue as a distinct test scenario on SoSBench-Lite (Table 10). SciSafeEval samples also join the semantic comparison in Figure 3.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add GPT-5 and Intern-S1, while Claude-4-Opus variants are replaced by Claude-4.1-Opus variants. The evaluator comparison removes GPT-4.1-mini and adds o4-mini, o3 and GPT-5 alongside retained evaluators. Figure 3 adds SciSafeEval as a comparator, and Appendix A.3 introduces a separate Crescendo attack comparison.

E3.justification: The primary evaluation switches from GPT-4.1-based Harmful Rate to GPT-5-based Policy Violation Rate, with substantively revised judgment criteria rather than just a renamed metric. Existing generation budgets and default decoding settings remain. The new Crescendo experiment uses GPT-4.1 as adversary and scorer, with five maximum turns and two backtracks; new difficulty and task-type analyses use GPT-4.1 classification.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of comprehension versus answering difficulty, task composition, agreement between full and Lite evaluations, and robustness to multi-turn Crescendo attacks (Tables 4–6 and 10; Figure 6). These investigate previously untested questions. The existing unlearning study is retained and moved from the main text to Appendix A.3, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 presents point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v3 introduces systematic uncertainty reporting through 90% confidence intervals for overall scores in Tables 2–3 and error bars in Figure 5. Neither version supplies repeated-run or seed counts, and the Figure 5 bars are not separately defined; additional independent runs cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Many reported scores change under the revised scoring protocol: Table 2 replaces GPT-4.1's 0.473 HR with 0.503 PVR and Deepseek-R1's 0.791 with 0.849. Scaling and unlearning results also change substantially; Figure 4 replaces R1-Distill's increase below 8B with a monotonic decline. New results include full/Lite correlations of 0.997 and 0.990 and Crescendo PVRs of 0.927–0.953. These are not same-setting performance changes. The original single-turn jailbreak table remains numerically unchanged.

T1.justification: The coverage definitions, sampling weights and probability formula are retained. HR and PVR use the same average-indicator mathematical structure, despite changed evaluation criteria. No theorem, proof or formal assumption is added or revised; the confidence-interval formula belongs to statistical reporting.

C1.justification: v3 explicitly limits its scope to six selected, non-exhaustive scientific domains and frames the headline measurement as policy violations. It foregrounds the already-described synthesis framework in the contribution list. The central claims of a regulation-grounded benchmark and insufficient scientific safety alignment remain.

C2.justification: Finding 4 replaces the proposed 8B knowledge/alignment crossover with an explanation based on whether alignment scales alongside knowledge across model families. New interpretations explain uneven risk-category coverage, emphasize procedural misuse, and argue that single-turn safety does not reliably transfer to multi-turn dialogue. The conclusion adds limitations concerning incomplete domain coverage and the absence of severity-aware scoring.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a specific evaluation-code repository and project page, documents the PyRIT implementation and controls for Crescendo, and identifies the Chameleon computing testbed. It also provides the revised judge prompt and output schema. Existing seed collection and data-cleaning instructions are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for Intern-S1, Crescendo, PyRIT, JailbreakBench and output-centric safe completions. New Table 11 illustrates the claimed distinction from WMDP and SciSafeEval. The main related-work discussion and broader novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The title, author list, terminology and citation style change, with targeted rewrites of contributions, benchmark analysis, scaling interpretation and limitations. The appendices are reorganized and unlearning moves out of the main text. Most method and related-work prose, and the overall five-section narrative, are retained.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reformats the document with a new title layout, running headers, margins and caption/table styling. It adds difficulty/task tables, the Lite correlation plot, a Crescendo table and benchmark examples; expands the judge display; and relocates unlearning. Figure 3 gains SciSafeEval points and a legend entry, while Figure 5 gains error bars.

improvement.justification: The added difficulty/task characterization and Lite validation better support the benchmark's intended use, while uncertainty reporting and multi-turn testing strengthen the evidence. More explicit judge and attack specifications improve transparency. These gains are qualified by unreconciled reporting: the conclusion retains Deepseek-R1's old 79.1% rate despite Table 2 reporting 84.9%, and Figure 3 adds SciSafeEval without updating its sampling description. The judge change also prevents interpreting higher reported rates as same-setting changes in model safety.
